article_units.name: Theatre Roles and Stagecraft
article_units.subtitle: How a play comes to life: the people who make theatre, the spaces it happens in, and the languages of stagecraft.

lessons.title: Who Makes a Play: Roles in Professional Theatre
lessons.description: The director, performers, designers, stage manager and technicians, and what each contributes to a production.

lessons.title: The Designers' Toolkit: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
lessons.description: Design fundamentals such as scale, shape, colour and texture, and how each design discipline shapes meaning.
spec_references: 3.1.1 How meaning is interpreted and communicated

lessons.title: Theatre Spaces: Configuration and Audience
lessons.description: Proscenium, thrust, in-the-round, traverse, end-on and promenade configurations and how they shape an audience's experience.

lessons.title: Performer Skills: Voice and Body
lessons.description: Vocal qualities (pitch, pace, accent, intonation) and physical qualities (gesture, posture, movement) that shape character.

lessons.title: From Page to Stage: The Rehearsal Process
lessons.description: How directors, performers and designers collaborate from read-through to opening night, and the role of the stage manager.

article_units.name: Drama Practitioners and Styles
article_units.subtitle: Stanislavski, Brecht, Artaud, Frantic Assembly: the thinkers whose ideas shape modern theatre.

lessons.title: Stanislavski and Naturalism
lessons.description: Emotion memory, given circumstances, the magic if and the system that built modern naturalistic acting.

lessons.title: Brecht and Epic Theatre
lessons.description: Verfremdungseffekt, gestus, breaking the fourth wall, and theatre as a tool to make audiences think.

lessons.title: Artaud and Theatre of Cruelty
lessons.description: Ritual, sensory assault and total theatre that overwhelms the audience and shocks them awake.

lessons.title: Physical Theatre: Frantic Assembly and Beyond
lessons.description: Movement-led storytelling, ensemble, lifts, chair duets and how physical theatre communicates without words.

article_units.name: Live Theatre Review
article_units.subtitle: How to analyse a production you have seen: performers, designers, directorial choices, and effect on the audience.

lessons.title: Watching Theatre Critically: Taking Useful Notes
lessons.description: How to watch a live production with an analytical eye and capture the detail you need for the written exam.

lessons.title: Analysing Performers: Vocal and Physical Choices
lessons.description: Pinpointing the specific acting choices that communicate character and meaning to an audience.

lessons.title: Analysing Design: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
lessons.description: Reading design choices in a production and explaining the meanings they generate for the audience.

lessons.title: Effect on the Audience: Evaluation Beyond Description
lessons.description: Moving from describing what you saw to judging how successfully meaning was communicated and why.

article_units.name: The Crucible by Arthur Miller
article_units.subtitle: Salem 1692 as a mirror for McCarthyism: hysteria, conscience and the ruin of a community.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: A Four-Act Tragedy
lessons.description: How Miller structures the descent from rumour to courtroom to gallows across four escalating acts.

lessons.title: Characters and Relationships: Proctor, Abigail, Elizabeth
lessons.description: Major characters and the moral pressures, jealousies and loyalties that drive their choices.

lessons.title: Themes: Hysteria, Reputation, Conscience
lessons.description: How rumour, hypocrisy, integrity and the courage to refuse a lie weave through the play.

lessons.title: Context: Salem 1692 and McCarthy 1953
lessons.description: Puritan New England, Cold War America, and how Miller used history to indict his own moment.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Language and Genre
lessons.description: Miller's heightened Puritan idiom, public confrontation scenes and the conventions of moral tragedy.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Bringing Salem to the Stage
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that conjure a Puritan world and the suffocating courtroom.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Acting Proctor's Final Choice
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Proctor, Abigail and Elizabeth in the play's most charged scenes.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Brecht and the Crucible
lessons.description: Reading the play through Brechtian and Stanislavskian lenses and choosing the most useful approach.

article_units.name: Blood Brothers by Willy Russell
article_units.subtitle: Twins separated at birth on opposite sides of the British class divide, and the fate that draws them back together.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Two-Act Working-Class Tragedy
lessons.description: Russell's circular structure, framed by the Narrator, that returns the audience to its opening tableau.

lessons.title: Characters: Mickey, Edward, Mrs Johnstone, Mrs Lyons
lessons.description: The twins, their two mothers and the Narrator who watches fate close in on them.

lessons.title: Themes: Class, Fate, Nature versus Nurture
lessons.description: How postcode and luck shape lives, and whether biology or upbringing makes us who we are.

lessons.title: Context: Liverpool, Thatcher and the Working-Class Musical
lessons.description: 1980s Britain, deindustrialisation and the working-class voice Willy Russell brought to the West End.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: The Narrator and the Songs
lessons.description: How direct address, recurring motifs and music drive the audience towards the inevitable ending.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Two Worlds, One Stage
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that contrast the Johnstone and Lyons households.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Playing Mickey at Seven and Twenty-Five
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Mickey, Edward and Mrs Johnstone across the play's age leaps.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Brecht in Russell's Stage Directions
lessons.description: How Russell's narrator, songs and direct address show Brechtian influence inside a popular musical form.

article_units.name: Noughts and Crosses by Malorie Blackman / Dominic Cooke
article_units.subtitle: An alternate Britain where Crosses rule and noughts are second-class: race, segregation and forbidden love.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: A Dystopian Two-Act Tragedy
lessons.description: How Cooke's stage adaptation compresses Blackman's novel into a fast-moving political tragedy.

lessons.title: Characters: Sephy, Callum and Their Families
lessons.description: Two teenagers, their mothers and the political and personal tensions that pull them apart.

lessons.title: Themes: Race, Power, Love Across Lines
lessons.description: Reversed racial hierarchy, systemic injustice, terrorism, sacrifice and the cost of resistance.

lessons.title: Context: Blackman, Cooke and the Politics of Adaptation
lessons.description: Why Blackman wrote the novel, why the RSC staged it, and how the play speaks to contemporary Britain.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Direct Address and Dual Narration
lessons.description: Sephy and Callum's interlocking monologues, the use of news reports and the device of swapped power.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: World-Building on a Bare Stage
lessons.description: Set, projection, sound and costume choices that build an alternate Britain without naturalistic clutter.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Sephy and Callum's First Confrontation
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices that capture the inequality and intimacy between the two leads.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Brechtian Distance and Naturalistic Truth
lessons.description: How a director might balance epic-theatre political signposting with naturalistic emotional truth.

article_units.name: Around the World in 80 Days by Verne / Eason
article_units.subtitle: Phileas Fogg's Victorian wager turned into a high-speed feat of multi-roling and ensemble theatre.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Eight Actors, Eighty Days
lessons.description: Eason's stage adaptation of Verne's novel, structured as a chase across continents told by a small ensemble.

lessons.title: Characters: Fogg, Passepartout and a Cast of Many
lessons.description: Fogg's eccentric precision, Passepartout's energy, Fix's pursuit and the dozens of multi-roled minor parts.

lessons.title: Themes: Time, Empire and Adventure
lessons.description: Victorian fascination with steam, schedule and global mastery, and what a modern stage can say about it.

lessons.title: Context: Verne in 1872, Eason in 2013
lessons.description: The Victorian novel, its 19th-century travel craze, and how a modern adaptation reframes the journey.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Multi-roling, Mime and Storytelling
lessons.description: How a small cast becomes elephants, trains and crowds through narration, sound and physical theatre.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: A World on a Bare Stage
lessons.description: How chairs, ropes and lighting become trains, ships and elephants in a high-energy ensemble production.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Comic Precision and Ensemble Trust
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Fogg, Passepartout and the company across the play's most demanding sequences.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Physical Theatre and Ensemble Storytelling
lessons.description: Frantic Assembly, Complicite and the storytelling traditions a director can borrow from to stage Verne.

article_units.name: Things I Know to Be True by Andrew Bovell
article_units.subtitle: Four siblings, two parents and the quiet revelations that crack open an Australian suburban family.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Four Seasons, Four Children
lessons.description: How Bovell shapes the play around the seasons and gives each child their own central revelation.

lessons.title: Characters: The Price Family
lessons.description: Bob and Fran as parents, and Pip, Mark, Ben and Rosie navigating identity and their parents' expectations.

lessons.title: Themes: Family, Identity, Truth
lessons.description: Love, conditional acceptance, gender identity, financial wrongdoing, infidelity and the distance between generations.

lessons.title: Context: Bovell, Frantic Assembly and 2016 Adelaide
lessons.description: Bovell's career, the Frantic Assembly co-production and the play's contemporary Australian setting.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Monologue and Movement
lessons.description: How Bovell weaves naturalistic dialogue with direct-address monologues, and how movement carries subtext.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: The Garden and the Kitchen
lessons.description: Set, lighting and sound choices that move between domestic interior and the symbolic garden of memory.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Bob's Final Tableau
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Bob, Fran and the four children in the play's most charged moments.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Stanislavski Meets Frantic Assembly
lessons.description: How naturalistic acting and physical-theatre movement coexist in Bovell's hybrid play.

article_units.name: Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare
article_units.subtitle: Verona, two warring houses and the tragedy of teenagers who love against the world.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Five Acts, One Week
lessons.description: How Shakespeare compresses the lovers' courtship, marriage and deaths into roughly five frantic days.

lessons.title: Characters: Lovers, Families, Friends
lessons.description: Romeo, Juliet, the Nurse, Mercutio, Tybalt, Friar Lawrence and the parents whose feud kills their children.

lessons.title: Themes: Love, Fate, Honour, Youth and Age
lessons.description: Romantic, familial and sexual love; the stars; the feud as inherited rage; and the gap between generations.

lessons.title: Context: Shakespeare's Verona and London
lessons.description: Renaissance Italy, the Elizabethan playhouse, source material and the original audiences who watched it.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Verse, Prose and the Sonnet
lessons.description: Iambic pentameter, the sonnet shared by the lovers, the Nurse's prose and how the verse signals character.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Verona Then and Now
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices for traditional, modern and concept productions.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: The Balcony and the Tomb
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Romeo, Juliet, Mercutio and Tybalt in the play's most pivotal scenes.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Naturalism vs Heightened Style
lessons.description: Choosing between psychological realism and a more stylised, ritualistic approach to Shakespeare's verse.

article_units.name: A Taste of Honey by Shelagh Delaney
article_units.subtitle: Salford, 1958: a working-class teenager, her unreliable mother and the friends who stand in for family.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Two Acts, One Damp Flat
lessons.description: Delaney's two-act kitchen-sink drama, framed by Helen's arrivals and departures from Jo's life.

lessons.title: Characters: Jo, Helen, Geof, Peter, Boy
lessons.description: A teenager finding herself between an absent mother, a kind queer friend and a brief sailor lover.

lessons.title: Themes: Class, Motherhood, Race, Sexuality
lessons.description: Working-class life, single motherhood, interracial romance and queer friendship at the edge of acceptability.

lessons.title: Context: Salford 1958 and the Kitchen-Sink Movement
lessons.description: Post-war working-class Britain, Theatre Workshop, Joan Littlewood and Delaney as the teenage outsider.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Direct Address, Music and Comedy
lessons.description: Delaney's bold use of direct address, jazz interludes and tonal swings between comedy and pain.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Damp Walls and Bright Light
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that capture the squalor and unexpected beauty of Jo's flat.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Jo and Helen's Final Scene
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Jo, Helen, Geof and Peter in their most emotionally loaded confrontations.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Theatre Workshop and Brechtian Direct Address
lessons.description: How Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop shaped the original production and how its devised, Brechtian methods still serve the play.

article_units.name: The Great Wave by Francis Turnly
article_units.subtitle: Two countries, two decades: a Japanese family searches for a daughter abducted by North Korea.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: A Tale Across Two Countries
lessons.description: How Turnly tracks parallel timelines in Japan and North Korea over almost three decades.

lessons.title: Characters: The Hashimoto Family and Their Captors
lessons.description: Etsuko, Hanako, their mother Etsuko Sr, Reiko and the North Korean officials and detainees they meet.

lessons.title: Themes: State Power, Identity, Family Loss
lessons.description: Authoritarianism, abduction as policy, identity under coercion, and the long ache of ambiguous loss.

lessons.title: Context: Japan, North Korea and the Real Abductions
lessons.description: Verified Japanese citizens abducted by North Korea, Cold War politics and the play's documentary roots.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Cross-Cutting and Stage Directions
lessons.description: How Turnly cross-cuts between Japan and North Korea and uses stage directions to suggest the sea.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Sea, State Apartment and Searchlight
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that move between Japanese coast and North Korean compound.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Hanako Across Twenty Years
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Hanako, Reiko and the family that age them across decades.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Documentary Theatre and Brecht
lessons.description: Reading the play as documentary verbatim or as Brechtian political theatre, and choosing between them.

article_units.name: The Empress by Tanika Gupta
article_units.subtitle: Victorian Britain through Indian eyes: an ayah on the docks, an Indian MP at Westminster, and Queen Victoria's munshi.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Two Worlds, One Empire
lessons.description: How Gupta interweaves Rani's London survival story with Abdul Karim's rise at Queen Victoria's court.

lessons.title: Characters: Rani, Abdul, Hari, Lascar and Queen
lessons.description: An ayah, the Queen's munshi, an Indian MP, a Lascar sailor and the British figures whose worlds they enter.

lessons.title: Themes: Empire, Race, Servitude, Solidarity
lessons.description: Imperial power, hidden Indian lives in Victorian Britain, and the solidarity that grows in the margins.

lessons.title: Context: Victorian Britain and the Indian Diaspora
lessons.description: 1887 Jubilee Britain, ayahs and Lascars in London, Abdul Karim at court and the early South Asian diaspora.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Languages, Letters and Songs
lessons.description: Bilingual exchanges, period letters, songs and direct address to bring hidden histories to the stage.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Docks, Drawing Rooms and Court
lessons.description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that move between East London streets and royal interiors.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Rani Standing Her Ground
lessons.description: Vocal and physical choices for Rani, Abdul, Hari and Queen Victoria in the play's pivotal scenes.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Brecht and Documentary History
lessons.description: Using Brechtian techniques to make hidden histories visible, and Stanislavski to ground individual lives.

unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Fresh build. AQA's set play list is distinct from Unity OCR Drama (Blood Brothers and Rise Up only). OCR content is bespoke teacher-PPT material under different licensing and not reusable for free tier.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students retell what happened in the production scene by scene rather than analysing how meaning was communicated through specific performer or design choices and why those choices worked for the audience.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 teacher resources, Live Theatre guidance — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/understanding-drama

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer set-play questions as essay-style literary analysis rather than as a performer or designer making concrete physical, vocal, lighting, sound, set or costume choices for a specific moment.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 specification, Section B requirements — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/scheme-of-assessment

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe design ideas in general terms (a dark mood, period costume) rather than naming specific elements such as lantern type, gobo, fabric, colour, fitting and the meaning each generates.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 mark scheme conventions and theatrical skills guidance — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/guidance-on-theatrical-skills

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write 'I would say it angrily' without specifying volume, pace, pitch, pause, gesture, posture, facial expression or proxemics for the named moment.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 specification, performer skills — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/guidance-on-theatrical-skills

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe a practitioner's biography but do not apply the techniques to a specific moment of the set play or live production.
common_misconceptions.source: Britannica entry on Brecht and the alienation effect — britannica.com/art/alienation-effect; Britannica entry on epic theatre — britannica.com/art/epic-theatre

student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain Effect: Students name a design element but do not explain its effect on the audience or its link to character, theme or context.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Interpret as Performer: Students describe what their character is feeling without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices anchored to a named moment of the play.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Interpret as Designer: Students give one design idea per skill (lighting, sound, set, costume) but do not justify the choice with reference to the moment's meaning or the designer's intention.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Analyse Intentions: Students describe events in the play instead of analysing what the playwright is trying to make the audience think, feel or understand at that moment.
student_errors_by_question_type.20 marks — Extended Staging Response: Students drift off the named focus of the question and write a general staging answer; they also under-use the extract, treating it as a prompt rather than reading specific lines and stage directions.
student_errors_by_question_type.32 marks — Live Theatre Review: Students retell plot rather than evaluating specific performer or design choices, and they fail to make a justified judgement about how successfully meaning was communicated to the audience.

topic_weighting_notes: The set-play section (Section B equivalent) carries 44 of 80 marks on the written paper — set-play units must be the most detailed and most rehearsed in the curriculum. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/specification-at-a-glance

The live theatre review carries 32 of 80 marks. Treat Unit 3 as a generic-skills unit because each student writes about a production they have personally seen, not a prescribed text. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/scheme-of-assessment

Theatre roles and stagecraft (Section A equivalent) carries only 4 of 80 marks but underpins every other answer because students must use the correct stagecraft vocabulary throughout. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/specification-at-a-glance
current_spec_changes: Specification version 1.7 (26 April 2022) is current; the nine prescribed plays remain unchanged. Source: specs/aqa/drama-8261-8261.md frontmatter and AQA specification page — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification

From 2019 onwards students must experience at least one live performance; digital streamings are no longer sufficient as the only experience. Source: AQA specification 8261, Area of study 2 — Live theatre production
pedagogical_notes: Drama benefits from regular, low-stakes retrieval of stagecraft vocabulary and practitioner techniques. Build retrieval activities into every set-play lesson and every revision technique guide. Source: Education Endowment Foundation Arts Participation summary — educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/arts-participation

Pair text-based study with brief practical activity (read a moment, stand it up, discuss the choices) — practical engagement raises attainment in extended-response writing about the same moment. Source: National Theatre Learn — nationaltheatre.org.uk/learn-explore/schools/teacher-resources/

For live theatre review, teach a What/How/Why scaffolding so students always describe the choice, explain how it created meaning and judge why it worked or did not. Source: National Theatre teacher resources for GCSE Drama — nationaltheatre.org.uk/learn-explore/schools/teacher-resources/gcse-drama-resources-for-set-texts/

drama_content_rules.perform_or_design_lens: Every set-play lesson must teach students to think as performer AND as designer for at least one named moment. Worked examples and exam-tip blocks must include both vocal/physical choices and at least one design discipline (lighting, sound, set or costume).
drama_content_rules.stage_terminology_required: Every set-play lesson should use and gloss stage-craft terms: stage left/right, upstage/downstage, blocking, proxemics, levels, focus, gestus, tableau, naturalistic vs stylised, lighting state/wash/special/gobo, sound cue, costume choice for character, set design, props as symbols.
drama_content_rules.no_plot_reproduction: Lessons must NEVER paraphrase the plot scene-by-scene or quote more than 15 words from any in-copyright play. Reference moments by name only (e.g. 'the moment Mickey learns the truth in Blood Brothers' or 'the linen scene in The Crucible') without reproducing dialogue.
drama_content_rules.quotation_cap_strict: Maximum 15 words from any in-copyright play, maximum once per lesson, in quotation marks. Better: paraphrase the situation. Public-domain Shakespeare (Romeo and Juliet) may be quoted more freely but still keep quotes short and purposeful.
drama_content_rules.practice_question_stems: Practice question stems must ask about staging, performance or design moments without reproducing the playwright's text. GOOD: 'How might a director use lighting to emphasise the shift in mood when Mickey learns the truth in Blood Brothers?' BAD: 'Mickey says "[long quote]". How does the writer...'
drama_content_rules.live_theatre_review_unit_only_generic: Unit 3 'Live Theatre Review' must teach generic skills only. Worked examples must use FICTIONAL productions (e.g. 'imagine you saw a production of [public-domain or named play] where the director chose...') because each student writes about their own production. Never reference specific real productions students may not have seen.
drama_content_rules.practitioner_application_per_play: Each set-play unit must include a practitioner-application lesson. Crucible: Brecht for political distance, Stanislavski for Proctor's interior. Blood Brothers: Brechtian narrator, Stanislavski for the leads. Noughts and Crosses: Brechtian distance plus naturalistic intimacy. Around the World in 80 Days: physical theatre, Frantic Assembly, ensemble. Things I Know to Be True: Stanislavski plus Frantic Assembly hybrid (Bovell co-developed with Frantic Assembly). Romeo and Juliet: verse-speaking technique vs heightened style. A Taste of Honey: Theatre Workshop (Joan Littlewood), Brechtian elements (live music, direct address). The Great Wave: documentary theatre and Brechtian witness. The Empress: Brechtian framing of hidden histories with Stanislavskian individual truth.
drama_content_rules.copyright_sensitivity_per_play: Romeo and Juliet is public domain (Shakespeare died 1616). All other 8 plays are in copyright: strict 15-word cap, prefer paraphrase, never reproduce plot. Reference Methuen, Nick Hern and Palgrave editions for context only — never reproduce their editorial notes or page numbers.
drama_content_rules.copyright_drift_grep: Validator hard-bans: 'Award\s+\d+\s+marks\s+for', 'Level [1-9]', 'Component \d', paper codes (8261/W, 8261/C, 8261/X), 'Section A', 'Section B', 'Section C', and verbatim AQA stems. Use StudyVault rubric (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging) for all 8+ mark levels-based mark schemes.
drama_content_rules.glossary_density: Aim for 6 or more inline `<dfn class="term">` glossary entries per lesson. Drama is heavy in stagecraft and practitioner terminology so this is easy to hit; do not pad with non-drama terms.
drama_content_rules.plain_text_rule: Plain unicode in description, practice_questions, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions, glossary_terms. HTML entities only in *_html fields (content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html).

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: An actor's job is not to feel — it is to make the audience feel.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Constantin Stanislavski

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Art is not a mirror held up to reality, but a hammer with which to shape it.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Bertolt Brecht

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The stage is a magic circle where only the most real things happen.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Peter Brook

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Theatre is the art of looking at ourselves.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Augusto Boal

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Stories are how we know ourselves; theatre is how we share that knowing.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Tanika Gupta

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Don't chase a play; let it come to you.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Mike Leigh

gaps: Devising drama (Component 2) and Texts in practice (Component 3) are practical/coursework components and are not covered in this article-only revision build. Students do those with their teacher; the platform supports the written paper only.
